column1: # The claims register: one row per thing this project says about itself, with a
# check a machine runs. Read by tools/check_claims.py - that script's docstring
# says what a row means, what the six check kinds are, and why this fails in
# both directions (a `built` claim that stopped holding, and an `open` gap that
# closed and left the row stale).
# Columns: id <TAB> claim <TAB> check <TAB> state <TAB> source
#   state is `built` (true of the code today), `open` (a real gap - the check
#   currently fails) or `unverifiable` (no definite check exists; the reason is
#   in the check column, beginning with "no definite check").
#   The check is written as evidence FOR the claim, so an `open` row usually
#   greps for the thing that does not exist yet, and a row about stale prose
#   carries an `absent` for the sentence that should be gone.
#   source is where the claim came from - file and line - so the original can
#   be read. Every line number was right when its row was written, and the
#   sources in buckets C and D were re-read after the prose corrections below
#   moved them (2026-10-05). Buckets A and B were re-read on 2026-10-15: the
#   A rows had been left pointing at prose that was never theirs when the queue
#   moved out of CLAUDE.md into docs/DECISIONS.md, so all 38 now point into the
#   queue itself (:1708-1747), or at the backups bullet for A37 and A38; and
#   three B rows were re-pointed at the line their claim actually rests on.
# Bucket A is CLAUDE.md's "Owner decisions recorded, not yet built" queue
# (CLAUDE.md:1812-1849), the list that misled a reader twice. Bucket B is
# build-status sentences already written down in docs/audit-reports-*/ and
# Bucket C is the rest of the documentation tree, swept on 2026-10-05 because
# the first register only covered A and B: the design docs' own "Status:" lines,
# the READMEs, the studio agents' brief (.claude/agents/JARVIS-TODAY.md), the
# living documents (ARCHITECTURE.md, JARVIS-API.md, CHANGELOG.md, VERSION), the
# build queue and the handoffs. Bucket D is the other direction of wrongness -
# a sentence claiming something IS done when it is not - and its first row is
# `no-file:`, the kind added for it: docs/README.md records the source bundle as
# removed on 2026-10-05 while the file is still in the tree and still tracked.
# A missing file could not be written down with `file:` (which asserts the
# opposite) or with `absent:` (which needs the path to exist first).
# Bucket E is the setup this project ships for a tool it needs installed
# (2026-10-09): SearXNG, the default web-search provider, brought up by
# docker/searxng/docker-compose.yml. Its rows exist because the compose file
# and the code that calls the container are two files that can drift apart
# silently - the port it publishes against the address jarvis_search.py
# calls, and the one SearXNG setting Jarvis cannot work without (json in the
# Bucket F is the model-facing settings tool (2026-10-13). The field test found
# the model would not call it, and the fix left two sentences this project now
# says about itself: the tool IS offered on a fresh install by the shipped
# `[tools].enabled` list, and its description is an instruction to call it (in
# the owner's own phrasings) rather than a note about the tool. Both are things
# a later edit could quietly take away, which is what a row is for.

the reader the snapshot-encryption checker uses is measured and not assumed: a plain file is never reported encrypted, and on Windows `cipher /e` on a folder really does set the folder's own EFS attribute and really does encrypt a file created in it afterwards (added 2026-10-14, with the EFS turn-on recorded in docs/SNAPSHOT-ENCRYPTION.md; the measurement itself needs Windows and this register is only ever evaluated on Linux - the audit job at ci.yml:1498 and the required backend job both run on ubuntu-latest - so this row pins the self-test's own proof in the tool's source rather than running a tool that cannot answer here)

the personal-data backup tool makes no network call at all - no socket, no urllib, no http, no requests - checked by reading its own source, so a later "send it to the cloud" option cannot be added without this suite going red

a snapshot of the owner's data is a consistent SQLite copy taken by SQLite itself with the write-ahead log folded in, not a file copy, so it is safe while Jarvis is running and a plain copy's lost databases cannot happen
the data backup never writes into the folder it reads: the destination and every restore target inside it are refused, so a typo cannot turn a backup into a write over the live data
every snapshot is verified by opening it again - integrity_check, the same set of tables the live database had, and no table holding fewer rows - and one that fails is never counted as a backup

both kinds of backup have ONE destination: the weekly personal-data snapshot tool reads the `folder` key of `~/.openjarvis/backup.json` at run time - the same key the app's own .jbak backups are written through - so a backup never goes somewhere the owner did not choose and two features cannot disagree about where his backups are
changing the folder changes where the NEXT weekly run writes, because the task's own command line names no destination and the key is read at run time, not baked into the registered task
a chosen backup folder inside the folder being backed up is refused in plain words and NOTHING is created there - not even the note recording the failure
